description: A team from University of Manchester
summary: NASA SPHEREx WebViewer is an interactive deep-sky explorer for NASA's SPHEREx mission, which surveys the entire sky in 102 near-infrared bands. We built a Python/Flask backend that queries the IPAC IRSA archive on demand, reprojects FITS cutouts onto a uniform sky grid, subtracts zodiacal light, and renders Lupton asinh false-colour tiles, paired with a Next.js/React frontend built on Aladin Lite for smooth pan and zoom. The challenge is access: SPHEREx data is enormous, stored as raw FITS files, and effectively unusable without specialist astronomy software. By partitioning the sky into ~1° cells and caching searches, cutouts and rendered tiles, the viewer turns archival data into a responsive browser experience with coordinate search, time and bandpass filters, multi-epoch comparison and a guided discovery tour. It matters because it makes cutting-edge infrared survey data explorable by students, educators and researchers, lowering the barrier to studying cosmic dust, ices and the history of the universe.
details:
What it does and how it works

SPHEREx Sky Viewer turns archived SPHEREx observations into an interactive false-colour sky map.

  1. Sky grid and on-demand loading. The backend organises the sky into approximately degree-scale cells. The frontend requests cells covering the current field of view, capped at 2°, keeping requests focused on the region the user is exploring.
  2. Archive search. The backend queries NASA/IPAC IRSA’s SIA2 services for observations in the spherex_dr1 and spherex_qr3 collections. Date-range and detector-pair filters determine which observations are eligible. Each cell displays its newest matching exposure, so neighbouring cells may represent different observation times.
  3. Image preparation. The backend reads the IMAGE and ZODI extensions of FITS cutouts and subtracts the supplied zodiacal-light model. A MAD-based filter suppresses unusually low pixel values, and weighted Gaussian interpolation fills small holes for display. These steps support visual exploration rather than precision photometry.
  4. Spatial alignment. A custom bilinear resampling implementation maps cutouts onto a common tangential (TAN) WCS grid. This places observations using their sky coordinates despite differences in orientation. Areas without valid coverage remain transparent, so gaps can still appear.
  5. False-colour rendering. Short- and long-wavelength detectors are paired into blue and red channels, with green calculated from their average. A Lupton asinh stretch maps the data into a displayable colour range. Users can adjust individual RGB weights and overall brightness. The colours represent infrared data; they are not natural-colour photographs.
  6. Interactive viewing. Aladin Lite provides pan and zoom. The interface includes coordinate navigation, date and detector-pair filters, nearby observation metadata, loading indicators, image inversion and a four-step guided tour.

Benefits

  • Accessible exploration: users can inspect real mission imagery without manually downloading FITS files or installing astronomy software.
  • Reduced repeated work: caches store search results, FITS cutouts and rendered PNG tiles. Locks prevent duplicate tile generation, while bounded concurrency and a centre-prioritised loading queue manage requests.
  • Flexible visual inspection: users can revisit a region with different date ranges, detector pairs and display settings.
  • Reproducible deployment: Docker Compose, health checks and a persistent cache volume support running the application on another server.
  • Room to extend: command-line tools for prewarming tiles and building WCS-based mosaics support further development.

Intended impact

The project aims to make SPHEREx imagery easier to explore for students, educators, amateur astronomers and other curious users. It brings archive retrieval, coordinate alignment and interactive display into one interface.

For the Planet X and SPHEREx challenge, this provides a foundation for exploring observations from different periods. The current prototype supports manual inspection; it does not automatically detect moving objects or identify new planets.

Tools and technologies

  • Backend: Python, Flask, NumPy, SciPy, Pillow, Astropy and Astroquery, with custom bilinear resampling and mosaic co-addition code.
  • Frontend: Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, shadcn/Base UI components, Aladin Lite and next-themes.
  • Infrastructure: Docker and Docker Compose, with a persistent cache volume.
  • Data: SPHEREx observations and FITS cutouts accessed through NASA/IPAC IRSA.
  • Hardware: conventional server infrastructure and a WebGL-capable browser; no specialised user hardware is required.

What makes it creative

We adapt the familiar tiled-map approach to SPHEREx observations, combining spatially aligned imagery with observation filters and adjustable false-colour rendering.

The detector-pair mapping gives users a practical way to explore infrared information visually. Synthetic green connects the two input channels, while RGB controls allow users to change their relative emphasis. Guided exploration and observation metadata help explain what users are seeing.

The contribution is the integration of these capabilities into an approachable browser experience, supported by a backend that retrieves and processes images on demand.

Factors the team considered

  • Archive load: bounded concurrency and caching reduce repeated requests to IRSA.
  • Latency: on-demand processing limits initial work, while cached results accelerate repeat visits.
  • Scientific interpretation: false colours, synthetic green and display interpolation must be distinguished from independent spectral measurements.
  • Coverage: available imagery depends on the selected dates, detector pair and overlapping observation footprints.
  • Usability: coordinate controls, guided steps and metadata help users navigate unfamiliar astronomical data. Clearer distinctions between loading failures and missing coverage remain a priority.
  • Scope: the field-of-view cap limits the amount of data requested at once. Explicit comparisons between epochs and independent wavelength selection are future extensions.
